titleStmt.title: To Harriet Shaw Weaver. Friday, 8 December 1922
titleStmt.author: James Joyce

seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Dear Miss Weaver: My sight has been very changeable all this week. Today I can’t write all I want to say. It is very irritating. I continue with Dr Borsch to whom I presented Ulysses . He ought to cure me and he says he will. He says he would not operate the eye if possible for two months (!) and in the meantime the dental abscess under it at least ought to be removed – not that it is the cause but an activity of the abscess after operation might ruin his work: O dear me! How very monotonous.

Many thanks for your cheque (frs 6450) in payment of royalties. I read Mr Hueffer’s article which if not dictated at least carries out your keyword. I shall write to thank him. Yes, Mrs Murray should get a copy and I think copies might be sent to two men of letters who interested themselves in me in my youth – Mr Arthur Symons and Mr William Archer. I got the leaflets but did not see Mr Clement Shorter’s name among the critics. Will you please add to group the name at foot of this letter? I think you could send copies of the English Review to the following names (I omit their titles): Joyce, Murray , Healy, Jaloux, Larbaud, Quinn. As regards Mr Quinn, I dislike association with Mr Sumner . I think an injunction should be lodged at once in your name (as holder of the American rights). This does not pledge to a legal action. At the same time I think responsible critics and journalists who are in my favour ought to be informed. Something ought to be done at once. I don’t think the copies of which Mr Rodker speaks will have more than a temporary effect.
I am wondering whether your odyssey round London has been undertaken in the hope of surprising detective sergeant King Beaver curled up asleep round a lamppost in loneliest London?
I am to see Mr Larbaud today. If he has any news I will let you know.

div.note: Borsch would not operate on JJ’s eyes until April 1923 when he performed a sphincterectomy (JJ 543).

Before Borsch could proceed with a sphincterectomy, he required the complete extraction of JJ’s teeth. Six or seven of JJ’s decayed teeth were extracted on 4 April 1923, with the rest of them a few days later (JJ 543).

After requests from Pound and Weaver, Ford Madox Ford (Ford Madox Hueffer) published an essay in The English Review (“Ulysses and the Handling of Indecencies”), defending the book against charges of obscenity. Ford would later write that Sylvia Beach also forced him to defend Ulysses, “That untiring lady battered me without ceasing. She demanded that I should write innumerable articles about Ulysses” (qtd. in Joseph Wiesenfarth, “Fargobawlers: James Joyce and Ford Madox Ford”, Biography 14, no. 2 (Spring 1992), 95-116, esp. 114.
JJ similarly wrote, in another letter to Weaver (25 November 1922) that Ford “apologized in a way for his article which, he says, was written at your dictation” (LIII 69).

The leaflet Extracts from Press Notices of Ulysses by James Joyce, printed in Harlesden by Leveridge & Company, was issued in December 1922. Though Shorter’s name was not provided, his words from “A Literary Letter: ‘As Flat as a Page by C.K.S.’” (The Sphere 90, no. 1172 [8 July 1922]: 50) were quoted: “the maddest, muddiest, most loathsome book issued in our own or any other time — inartistic, incoherent, unquotably nasty — a book that one would have thought could only emanate from a criminal lunatic asylum”.

JJ wrote to his Aunt Josephine Murray in a letter on 21 December 1922, “I suppose you received the Criterion and English Review”, the former with Larbaud’s article and the latter in which Ford’s article features (35, no. 169 [December 1922], 538-48).
In October 1920 John Sumner successfully brought action against The Little Review , in which the “Nausicaa” episode of Ulysses had been serialised (7, no. 2 [July-August 1920], 42-58).

The “King Beaver” reference has been instrumental in dating the earliest notes for “Work in Progress”. In early November 1922, as the London police suspected Weaver of smuggling forbidden books into England, she told JJ she feared that her house was being watched by a plain clothes policeman. JJ dictated a reply on 8 November (written by Lucia): “That solitary detective is an interesting figure. Is he what the English call a king Beaver, that is an Irish constabulariman with red whiskers, riding a red bicicle?” (LI 193; Lucia’s spelling; BL Add. 57346). The first page of the first Finnegans Wake notebook contains the jotting: “King Beaver redwhiskered / policeman on a / green bicycle” (VI.B.10.001). The source for this note is a reader’s response to an article in the Irish Times ([20 October 1922], 6), called “Beaveritis”, about a game that had become popular in England (to be played by two people using a scoring system borrowed from tennis; the player who first cried “Beaver!” as soon as a bearded person appeared, scored). According to the article in the Irish Times, a “Royal Beaver” is a man afflicted with a full outfit of face-fittings – to wit, beard and moustache – while a “King Beaver” is a red-whiskered policeman riding a green bicycle” (source identified by Vincent Deane).

One of Larbaud’s plans was to start working, in February 1923, on “Fragments d’Ulysse – that is the translation of certain parts of Ulysses and their publication in book form here in a limited edition” (LI 199).
